PSE II · Chapter 29

Electromagnetic Induction

A changing flux makes an EMF

← PSE II Course

29.0 — The Discovery That Changed Everything

In Chapters 22–25, we saw that stationary charges create electric fields. In Chapter 28, we saw that steady currents create magnetic fields. But the deepest question in electromagnetism was still unanswered: can a magnetic field create an electric current?

The answer came in 1831, and it came from a man with almost no formal mathematical training. Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was the son of a blacksmith who had been apprenticed to a bookbinder at age 14. He educated himself by reading the books he was binding, attended public lectures by Sir Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution, and eventually became Davy’s laboratory assistant. Within two decades, he had made more experimental discoveries than perhaps any other scientist in history.

“Nothing is too wonderful to be true, if it be consistent with the laws of nature.” — Michael Faraday, 1849

Faraday knew from Oersted’s 1820 discovery (Chapter 28) that electric currents produce magnetic fields. He spent ten years trying to reverse the process — to produce electric current from a magnetic field. On August 29, 1831, he finally succeeded: by thrusting a bar magnet into a coil of wire, he observed a brief pulse of current in a galvanometer. When he pulled the magnet out, current flowed in the opposite direction. When the magnet was stationary — even sitting inside the coil — no current flowed.

The key insight was not that a magnetic field produces current, but that a changing magnetic field produces current. Static fields, no matter how strong, produce nothing. It is the change that matters.

Independently and almost simultaneously, Joseph Henry (1797–1878) in the United States discovered the same phenomenon. Henry had actually observed induction a year earlier but had not published. The law bears Faraday’s name because he published first and developed the concept more thoroughly.

*Personal note: Faraday’s discovery is arguably the most consequential experiment in the history of technology. Every electrical generator, every transformer, every induction cooktop, every wireless charging pad, every electric guitar pickup — all trace directly to August 29, 1831. The modern electrical grid exists because of this principle.

29.1 — Magnetic Flux

Why Flux?

Before we can state Faraday’s Law precisely, we need a quantity that captures “how much magnetic field passes through a loop.” We encountered this idea briefly in Chapter 28 (Section 28.7) when discussing Gauss’s Law for magnetism. Now we develop it as a working tool.

Recall from Chapter 23 that we defined electric flux \(\Phi_E = \int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}\) to quantify how much electric field threads through a surface. The magnetic analog is identical in structure.

Definition

The magnetic flux through a surface is:

\[\boxed{\Phi_B = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = \int B\cos\theta\,dA}\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) and the area element \(d\vec{A}\) (the outward normal to the surface). The SI unit is the weber (Wb):

\[1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2\]

For a uniform field passing through a flat surface of area \(A\):

\[\boxed{\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta}\]

Physical Interpretation

Think of magnetic flux as the number of field lines threading through the loop. More precisely:

  • \(\theta = 0°\) (\(\vec{B}\perp\) loop plane, \(\vec{B}\parallel\hat{n}\)): \(\Phi_B = BA\) — maximum flux. The loop “catches” all the field lines.
  • \(\theta = 90°\) (\(\vec{B}\parallel\) loop plane, \(\vec{B}\perp\hat{n}\)): \(\Phi_B = 0\) — no flux. The field lines slide along the surface without piercing it.
  • \(\theta = 180°\): \(\Phi_B = -BA\) — maximum negative flux. The field lines thread through in the opposite sense.

The sign of the flux depends on which side of the surface we call “positive” (i.e., the direction of \(\hat{n}\)). For a closed surface, we use the outward normal by convention, and Gauss’s Law for magnetism guarantees \(\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0\). For an open surface bounded by a loop (which is what Faraday’s Law uses), the direction of \(\hat{n}\) is linked to the sense of traversal around the loop by the right-hand rule.

Flux Through a Coil of \(N\) Turns

If a coil has \(N\) identical turns, each turn intercepts approximately the same flux \(\Phi_B\). The total flux linkage is:

\[N\Phi_B\]

This quantity appears directly in Faraday’s Law and in the definition of inductance (Section 29.5).

Electric Flux vs. Magnetic Flux

Property Electric Flux (Ch 23) Magnetic Flux (Ch 28–29)
Definition \(\Phi_E = \int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}\) \(\Phi_B = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}\)
Units N\(\cdot\)m\(^2\)/C (or V\(\cdot\)m) Wb = T\(\cdot\)m\(^2\)
Through closed surface \(\Phi_E = Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0\) (can be \(\neq 0\)) \(\Phi_B = 0\) (always)
Physical meaning Net field lines leaving enclosed charge Field lines threading through a surface
Role in Maxwell’s equations Gauss’s Law Gauss’s Law for magnetism; Faraday’s Law

Example: Flux Through a Tilted Loop

A circular loop of radius \(r = 0.10\ \text{m}\) is placed in a uniform magnetic field \(B = 0.50\ \text{T}\). The normal to the loop makes an angle \(\theta = 30°\) with \(\vec{B}\).

Area: \(A = \pi r^2 = \pi(0.10)^2 = 3.14\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}^2\)

Flux: \(\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta = (0.50)(3.14\times10^{-2})\cos 30° = \boxed{1.36\times10^{-2}\ \text{Wb} = 13.6\ \text{mWb}}\)

If the loop is rotated to \(\theta = 0°\) (face-on): \(\Phi_B = 15.7\ \text{mWb}\). If tilted to \(\theta = 90°\) (edge-on): \(\Phi_B = 0\). The flux varies smoothly between these extremes as the loop rotates — and that variation is exactly what drives an electric generator.

Example: Flux Through a Solenoid Loop

A circular loop of radius \(r_\text{loop} = 0.15\ \text{m}\) surrounds a solenoid of radius \(r_\text{sol} = 0.050\ \text{m}\), \(n = 1000\ \text{turns/m}\), \(I = 3.0\ \text{A}\). The loop and solenoid share the same axis.

Key insight: The field inside the solenoid is \(B = \mu_0 nI = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(1000)(3.0) = 3.77\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}\), but the field is confined to the solenoid’s cross-section (\(B \approx 0\) outside). The flux through the loop uses the solenoid’s area, not the loop’s area:

\[\Phi_B = B(\pi r_\text{sol}^2) = (3.77\times10^{-3})\pi(0.050)^2 = \boxed{2.96\times10^{-5}\ \text{Wb} = 29.6\ \mu\text{Wb}}\]

Making the surrounding loop larger does not increase the flux — the extra area is in a region where \(B = 0\). This is a common conceptual trap: flux depends on where the field is, not just the area of the loop.

29.2 — Faraday’s Law of Induction

The Law

Faraday’s experiments revealed a precise quantitative relationship: the EMF induced in a loop is equal to the negative rate of change of the magnetic flux through the loop. For a coil of \(N\) turns:

\[\boxed{\mathcal{E} = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}}\]

This is Faraday’s Law of Induction — the third of Maxwell’s four equations (after Gauss’s Law and Gauss’s Law for magnetism from earlier chapters). The negative sign encodes Lenz’s Law (Section 29.3) and ensures conservation of energy.

For a single loop (\(N = 1\)):

\[\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}\]

What Can Change?

Since \(\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta\), the flux can change if any of the three factors change:

  1. The field magnitude \(B\) changes — e.g., turning up the current in a nearby electromagnet
  2. The area \(A\) changes — e.g., stretching or compressing the loop
  3. The angle \(\theta\) changes — e.g., rotating the loop in a fixed field (this is how generators work)

All three produce induced EMF. The physics does not care why the flux changes — only that it changes, and how fast.

The EMF Is Not Localized — and the Maxwell Form of Faraday’s Law

An induced EMF is fundamentally different from a battery EMF. A battery has a definite location — the EMF appears across its terminals. An induced EMF is distributed around the entire loop. There is no single point where the “voltage” lives. This is a profound distinction: Faraday’s Law tells us that a changing magnetic field creates an electric field that circulates in closed loops. This induced electric field is non-conservative — its line integral around a closed path is nonzero.

Writing \(\mathcal{E} = \oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}\) (the work per unit charge done by the electric field around the loop) and substituting into Faraday’s Law gives the field form of the law:

\[\boxed{\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}}\]

This is Faraday’s Law as Maxwell wrote it — the third of Maxwell’s four equations. The two forms are the same statement in different dress:

  • Circuit form \(\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt\) — what you use to compute EMFs in loops and coils.
  • Field form \(\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = -d\Phi_B/dt\) — the fundamental statement about how electric and magnetic fields are coupled in spacetime.

Compare the field form to the electrostatic field from Chapter 22, where \(\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = 0\) always. The electric field induced by a changing magnetic field is a genuinely new kind of electric field — it circulates rather than radiating from charges.

*Personal note: This is the moment where the neat separation of “electrostatics” and “magnetostatics” breaks down. Changing magnetic fields create electric fields; we will see in Chapter 31 that changing electric fields create magnetic fields. The two fields are coupled — they are aspects of a single electromagnetic field.

Example: EMF from a Changing Field

A circular loop of radius \(r = 0.080\ \text{m}\) (\(N = 1\)) lies in a region where the magnetic field is uniform and perpendicular to the loop. The field increases linearly from \(B_i = 0.20\ \text{T}\) to \(B_f = 0.80\ \text{T}\) over \(\Delta t = 0.50\ \text{s}\).

Flux at any time: \(\Phi_B = BA = B\pi r^2\)

Rate of change: \(d\Phi_B/dt = (dB/dt)\pi r^2 = \left(\frac{0.80 - 0.20}{0.50}\right)\pi(0.080)^2 = (1.20)(2.01\times10^{-2})\)

\[|\mathcal{E}| = \frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = \boxed{2.41\times10^{-2}\ \text{V} = 24.1\ \text{mV}}\]

If the loop has resistance \(R = 0.50\ \Omega\), the induced current is \(I = |\mathcal{E}|/R = 48.2\ \text{mA}\). The direction is determined by Lenz’s Law (next section).

Example: EMF in a Rotating Coil (The Generator)

A rectangular coil with \(N = 100\) turns, area \(A = 0.020\ \text{m}^2\), rotates at angular velocity \(\omega = 120\pi\ \text{rad/s}\) (3600 rpm) in a uniform field \(B = 0.50\ \text{T}\).

Flux: \(\Phi_B = BA\cos(\omega t)\)

Induced EMF:

\[\mathcal{E} = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = -N\frac{d}{dt}[BA\cos(\omega t)] = NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)\]

\[\boxed{\mathcal{E}(t) = \mathcal{E}_0\sin(\omega t)}\]

where the peak EMF is:

\[\mathcal{E}_0 = NBA\omega = (100)(0.50)(0.020)(120\pi) = \boxed{377\ \text{V}}\]

This is an AC generator — the fundamental device that produces alternating current. The frequency is \(f = \omega/(2\pi) = 60\ \text{Hz}\), standard North American line frequency. A rotating coil in a magnetic field naturally produces a sinusoidal voltage. This is not a design choice — it is a consequence of Faraday’s Law and the cosine dependence of flux on angle.

Limiting cases:

  • At \(\omega t = 0\) (loop face-on to \(\vec{B}\)): Flux is maximum but \(d\Phi_B/dt = 0\), so \(\mathcal{E} = 0\). Maximum flux does not mean maximum EMF.
  • At \(\omega t = \pi/2\) (loop edge-on to \(\vec{B}\)): Flux is zero but changing fastest, so \(\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{E}_0\). The EMF is maximum precisely when the flux is zero.

This 90-degree phase shift between flux and EMF is characteristic of all sinusoidal induction. It is analogous to position and velocity in simple harmonic motion: position is maximum when velocity is zero, and vice versa.

29.3 — Lenz’s Law

The Direction of the Induced Current

Faraday’s Law gives us the magnitude of the induced EMF. Lenz’s Law gives us the direction:

Lenz’s Law: The induced current flows in a direction such that its own magnetic field opposes the change in flux that caused it.

This is what the negative sign in Faraday’s Law encodes. It is not an independent law — it is a consequence of energy conservation applied to electromagnetic induction.

Why It Must Be So

Imagine Lenz’s Law were reversed — that the induced current reinforced the flux change. Then:

  1. Increasing flux would induce current that increases flux further.
  2. That further increase would induce more current.
  3. The process would run away, producing infinite current and infinite magnetic field from an initial perturbation.

This would violate conservation of energy. Lenz’s Law is nature’s way of ensuring that you cannot get something for nothing — the induced current always resists the change, requiring an external agent to do work to maintain the changing flux.

Applying Lenz’s Law — A Recipe

  1. Determine the direction of \(\vec{B}\) through the loop.
  2. Determine whether \(\Phi_B\) is increasing or decreasing.
  3. The induced \(\vec{B}_\text{induced}\) opposes the change:
    • If \(\Phi_B\) is increasing: \(\vec{B}_\text{induced}\) opposes the external \(\vec{B}\) (points opposite).
    • If \(\Phi_B\) is decreasing: \(\vec{B}_\text{induced}\) supports the external \(\vec{B}\) (points same direction).
  4. Use the right-hand rule to find the current direction that produces \(\vec{B}_\text{induced}\).

The Bar Magnet and the Loop

When you push the north pole of a bar magnet toward a conducting loop:

  • External \(\vec{B}\) points into the loop (away from the north pole toward the loop).
  • \(\Phi_B\) is increasing.
  • The induced current must create a field that opposes the increase — so \(\vec{B}_\text{induced}\) points back toward the magnet (out of the loop on the magnet side).
  • By the right-hand rule, the induced current flows counterclockwise (as seen from the magnet).
  • The loop acts like a magnet with its north pole facing the approaching north pole — it repels the incoming magnet.

When you pull the magnet away:

  • \(\Phi_B\) is decreasing.
  • The induced current reverses, now creating a field that supports the disappearing flux.
  • The loop attracts the retreating magnet — it resists the departure.

In both cases, the loop fights the change. You must do work to push the magnet in and to pull it out. That work is converted into the electrical energy of the induced current, which is ultimately dissipated as heat in the loop’s resistance. Energy is conserved.

Example: Lenz’s Law with a Solenoid

A loop of wire surrounds a solenoid. The current in the solenoid is increasing, so the field inside the solenoid (and the flux through the loop) is increasing.

By Lenz’s Law: The induced current in the loop must oppose the increasing flux. The solenoid’s field points (say) to the right through the loop. The induced current must create a field pointing to the left through the loop. By the right-hand rule, the induced current flows clockwise (as viewed from the right).

Physical check: If you were holding the loop, you would feel a slight tug resisting the solenoid’s increasing field. To maintain the increasing current in the solenoid, the power supply must do extra work — some of its energy goes into driving the induced current in the surrounding loop.

29.4 — Motional EMF

A Conductor Moving Through a Magnetic Field

There is a beautifully intuitive way to understand Faraday’s Law that does not require any calculus of flux: consider the force on charges in a conductor that moves through a magnetic field.

A straight conductor of length \(L\) moves with velocity \(\vec{v}\) perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) (say, \(\vec{B}\) points into the page). The free electrons inside the conductor experience a magnetic force:

\[\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\]

This force pushes electrons toward one end of the conductor, leaving the other end positive. Charge accumulates until the electric field from the separated charges exactly balances the magnetic force:

\[qE = qvB \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad E = vB\]

The potential difference between the ends is:

\[\boxed{\mathcal{E} = BLv}\]

This is the motional EMF — a voltage that appears across a conductor simply because it moves through a magnetic field. No battery, no changing external field — just motion.

The Sliding Rail Problem

The most important application: a conducting rod slides at constant velocity \(v\) along parallel rails separated by distance \(L\), connected by a resistor \(R\) at one end, all in a uniform field \(\vec{B}\) (into the page).

As the rod moves, the area of the closed circuit increases: \(A = Lx\), where \(x\) is the rod’s position. The flux is \(\Phi_B = BLx\), and:

\[\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = -BL\frac{dx}{dt} = -BLv\]

The magnitude of the induced EMF is \(|\mathcal{E}| = BLv\), confirming our force-based derivation. The induced current is:

\[I = \frac{|\mathcal{E}|}{R} = \frac{BLv}{R}\]

By Lenz’s Law, the current flows counterclockwise (to oppose the increasing flux into the page). This current-carrying rod in the magnetic field experiences a braking force:

\[F = BIL = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R}\]

This force opposes the motion. To maintain constant velocity, an external agent must apply an equal force, doing work at rate:

\[P_\text{external} = Fv = \frac{B^2L^2v^2}{R}\]

The power dissipated in the resistor is:

\[P_R = I^2R = \frac{B^2L^2v^2}{R}\]

They are equal: all the mechanical work done by the external agent is converted to electrical energy dissipated as heat in the resistor. Energy conservation is satisfied exactly.

*Personal note: This is the physics of regenerative braking. When an electric car decelerates, the wheels drive a generator backward through the magnetic field. The braking force (which slows the car) does work that charges the battery instead of heating brake pads. The sliding rail is the same thing, stripped to its essence.

Example: Motional EMF on Sliding Rails

A rod slides at \(v = 5.0\ \text{m/s}\) on rails separated by \(L = 0.40\ \text{m}\) in a field \(B = 0.80\ \text{T}\). The resistance is \(R = 2.0\ \Omega\).

(A) Induced EMF:

\[|\mathcal{E}| = BLv = (0.80)(0.40)(5.0) = \boxed{1.6\ \text{V}}\]

(B) Induced current:

\[I = |\mathcal{E}|/R = 1.6/2.0 = \boxed{0.80\ \text{A}}\]

(C) Force required to maintain constant velocity:

\[F = BIL = (0.80)(0.80)(0.40) = \boxed{0.256\ \text{N}}\]

(D) Power balance:

\[P_\text{mech} = Fv = (0.256)(5.0) = 1.28\ \text{W}\]

\[P_R = I^2R = (0.80)^2(2.0) = 1.28\ \text{W} \quad \checkmark\]

Eddy Currents

When a bulk conductor (not just a thin wire) moves through a nonuniform magnetic field, the changing flux induces circulating currents throughout the conductor called eddy currents. These currents:

  • Flow in closed loops within the conductor
  • Obey Lenz’s Law: they create fields opposing the flux change
  • Produce a braking force that opposes the relative motion
  • Dissipate energy as \(I^2R\) heating in the conductor

Applications:

  • Magnetic braking: Drop a strong magnet through a copper tube — the magnet falls slowly because eddy currents create an upward force. No friction, no contact, no wear.
  • Induction cooktops: A rapidly alternating magnetic field induces eddy currents in the steel pot. The pot heats from \(I^2R\) losses while the cooktop surface stays cool.
  • Metal detectors: A coil produces an alternating field; eddy currents in a metal object alter the field pattern, which the detector senses.

Example: The Falling Magnet

A small neodymium magnet (mass \(m = 5.0\ \text{g}\)) is dropped through a vertical copper pipe. It reaches a terminal velocity of \(v_t = 0.10\ \text{m/s}\) (compared to free-fall speed after the same distance, which would be several m/s).

At terminal velocity, the magnetic braking force equals gravity:

\[F_\text{brake} = mg = (0.005)(9.8) = 0.049\ \text{N}\]

The power dissipated as heat in the copper pipe walls is:

\[P = F_\text{brake}\cdot v_t = (0.049)(0.10) = \boxed{4.9\ \text{mW}}\]

The gravitational potential energy of the magnet is being converted entirely into ohmic heating of the copper pipe — through electromagnetic induction with no physical contact between magnet and pipe.

29.5 — Inductance

Self-Inductance

Any current-carrying loop creates a magnetic field, and that field produces a flux through the loop itself. If the current changes, the self-flux changes, and by Faraday’s Law, an EMF is induced in the loop. This phenomenon is called self-induction, and the proportionality constant between flux linkage and current is the self-inductance (or simply inductance) \(L\):

\[\boxed{L = \frac{N\Phi_B}{I}}\]

The SI unit is the henry (H), named after Joseph Henry:

\[1\ \text{H} = 1\ \frac{\text{Wb}}{\text{A}} = 1\ \frac{\text{V}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{A}}\]

The self-induced EMF is:

\[\boxed{\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{dI}{dt}}\]

The negative sign (Lenz’s Law again) means the induced EMF opposes the change in current. When current is increasing (\(dI/dt > 0\)), the inductor opposes the increase. When current is decreasing (\(dI/dt < 0\)), the inductor opposes the decrease. An inductor resists any change in current — it has electromagnetic inertia.

Inductance of a Solenoid

The solenoid is the archetype inductor, just as the parallel-plate capacitor is the archetype capacitor. For a solenoid with \(N\) turns, length \(\ell\), cross-sectional area \(A\), and turns per unit length \(n = N/\ell\):

The field inside is \(B = \mu_0 nI\) (from Chapter 28). The flux through each turn is \(\Phi_B = BA = \mu_0 nIA\). The total flux linkage is \(N\Phi_B = (n\ell)(\mu_0 nIA) = \mu_0 n^2\ell A I\). Therefore:

\[\boxed{L = \mu_0 n^2 \ell A = \mu_0 n^2 V}\]

where \(V = \ell A\) is the volume of the solenoid. This can also be written as:

\[L = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{\ell}\]

The Grand Analogy — Inductor vs. Capacitor

This parallel is remarkable and worth studying carefully:

Property Capacitor (Ch 25) Inductor (Ch 29)
Stores energy in Electric field Magnetic field
Defining relation \(C = Q/\Delta V\) \(L = N\Phi_B/I\)
Geometry (ideal) \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\) (parallel plates) \(L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A\) (solenoid)
Energy stored \(U_E = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^2}{C}\) \(U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\)
Energy density \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\) \(u_B = \frac{1}{2}\frac{B^2}{\mu_0}\)
Opposes changes in Voltage (holds \(\Delta V\) constant) Current (holds \(I\) constant)
In DC steady state Open circuit (\(I = 0\)) Short circuit (\(\Delta V = 0\))
Characteristic equation \(I = C\,d(\Delta V)/dt\) \(\mathcal{E} = -L\,dI/dt\)
SI unit Farad (F) = C/V Henry (H) = V\(\cdot\)s/A

Both devices store energy in fields. The capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates; the inductor stores energy in the magnetic field inside its coils. The duality runs deep: every capacitor equation has an inductor counterpart with \(Q \leftrightarrow \Phi_B\), \(\Delta V \leftrightarrow I\), \(C \leftrightarrow L\), and \(\varepsilon_0 \leftrightarrow \mu_0\).

Example: Inductance of a Solenoid

A solenoid has \(N = 500\) turns, length \(\ell = 0.25\ \text{m}\), and radius \(r = 0.020\ \text{m}\).

Turns per unit length: \(n = N/\ell = 500/0.25 = 2000\ \text{turns/m}\)

Cross-sectional area: \(A = \pi r^2 = \pi(0.020)^2 = 1.26\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2\)

Inductance:

\[L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(2000)^2(0.25)(1.26\times10^{-3}) = \boxed{1.58\ \text{mH}}\]

This is a typical laboratory inductor. Millihenrys are common in electronics; henrys are rare and require very large coils.

Example: Self-Induced EMF

The solenoid above carries current that changes at \(dI/dt = 200\ \text{A/s}\).

\[|\mathcal{E}_L| = L\frac{dI}{dt} = (1.58\times10^{-3})(200) = \boxed{0.316\ \text{V}}\]

This “back-EMF” opposes the current change. In a circuit with a 12 V battery, this is a modest effect. But if you try to interrupt a large current through an inductor very quickly (\(dI/dt \to\) very large), the back-EMF can be enormous — this is why opening a switch on an inductive circuit produces a spark. The inductor “fights” the sudden current drop by producing whatever voltage is needed to maintain current flow, even if that means arcing across the switch gap.

Mutual Inductance

When two coils are near each other, a changing current in one induces an EMF in the other. The mutual inductance \(M\) quantifies this coupling:

\[\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\frac{dI_1}{dt} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathcal{E}_1 = -M\frac{dI_2}{dt}\]

where:

\[\boxed{M = \frac{N_2\Phi_{12}}{I_1} = \frac{N_1\Phi_{21}}{I_2}}\]

Here \(\Phi_{12}\) is the flux through coil 2 due to the current in coil 1. A remarkable theorem (the Neumann formula) guarantees that \(M\) is the same regardless of which coil is the source and which is the receiver.

The transformer is the most important application: two coils wound on a shared iron core with \(M\) close to its theoretical maximum. From Chapter 31, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: \(V_2/V_1 = N_2/N_1\). Transformers are why we can transmit electrical power over long distances — stepping up to high voltage for transmission (low \(I^2R\) losses) and stepping down for safe household use.

29.6 — RL Circuits

A New Kind of Transient

In Chapter 27, we studied RC circuits — a resistor and capacitor sharing a loop, producing exponential charging and discharging. Now we study RL circuits — a resistor and inductor sharing a loop. The mathematics is nearly identical, but the physics has a beautiful mirror symmetry.

In an RC circuit, the capacitor opposes changes in voltage. In an RL circuit, the inductor opposes changes in current.

Current Growth in an RL Circuit

Consider a battery \(\mathcal{E}\), a resistor \(R\), and an inductor \(L\) in series. At \(t = 0\), we close the switch.

At \(t = 0\): No current flows (\(I = 0\)). The inductor opposes the sudden appearance of current, so the entire battery voltage appears across the inductor: \(\mathcal{E}_L = \mathcal{E}\). The voltage across the resistor is \(V_R = 0\). The inductor initially acts like an open circuit.

As \(t\) increases: Current begins to flow, slowly at first (because the inductor resists the change). As current grows, \(V_R = IR\) increases and \(\mathcal{E}_L = \mathcal{E} - IR\) decreases. The inductor’s opposition weakens because \(dI/dt\) is getting smaller.

As \(t \to \infty\): Current reaches its steady-state value \(I_\text{max} = \mathcal{E}/R\). The inductor carries constant current (\(dI/dt = 0\)), so \(\mathcal{E}_L = 0\). The inductor acts like a short circuit (just a wire). All the battery voltage appears across the resistor.

Applying the loop rule at any time \(t\):

\[\mathcal{E} - IR - L\frac{dI}{dt} = 0\]

This is a first-order linear ODE. Its solution (verified by substitution) is:

\[\boxed{I(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau_L}\right) = I_\text{max}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau_L}\right)}\]

where the RL time constant is:

\[\boxed{\tau_L = \frac{L}{R}}\]

The voltage across the inductor decays exponentially:

\[\mathcal{E}_L(t) = \mathcal{E}\,e^{-t/\tau_L}\]

Current Decay in an RL Circuit

Now suppose steady-state current \(I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R\) flows, and we suddenly remove the battery (shorting the RL loop). The inductor opposes the disappearance of current. The loop rule gives \(L\,dI/dt + IR = 0\), with solution:

\[\boxed{I(t) = I_0\,e^{-t/\tau_L}}\]

The current decays exponentially with the same time constant \(\tau_L = L/R\).

The Time Constant: Dimensional Analysis

\[[\tau_L] = \frac{[L]}{[R]} = \frac{\text{H}}{\Omega} = \frac{\text{V}\cdot\text{s/A}}{\text{V/A}} = \text{s} \quad \checkmark\]

Compare to the RC time constant: \(\tau_{RC} = RC\) with \([\Omega][\text{F}] = \text{s}\). Both are products (or quotients) of the two circuit elements, yielding time.

*Personal note: The dimensional analysis reveals the physics. In an RC circuit, large \(R\) means slow charging (current trickles) and large \(C\) means lots of charge to move — both increase the time. In an RL circuit, large \(L\) means strong opposition to current change (electromagnetic inertia), increasing the time, while large \(R\) means the “friction” is high, which actually speeds up the approach to equilibrium — hence \(L/R\), not \(LR\).

The Grand Comparison — RC vs. RL Circuits

This is the capstone comparison table for this section. Every entry in the RC column has a mirror image in the RL column:

Property RC Circuit (Ch 27) RL Circuit (Ch 29)
Energy storage \(U = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2\) \(U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\)
Time constant \(\tau = RC\) \(\tau = L/R\)
Growth equation \(q(t) = Q_\text{max}(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) \(I(t) = I_\text{max}(1-e^{-t/\tau})\)
Decay equation \(q(t) = Q_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\) \(I(t) = I_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\)
What grows/decays Charge \(q\) (or voltage \(\Delta V_C\)) Current \(I\)
What decays/grows Current \(I\) Voltage \(\mathcal{E}_L\)
Element at \(t = 0\) acts like Short circuit (\(\Delta V_C = 0\)) Open circuit (\(I = 0\))
Element at \(t = \infty\) acts like Open circuit (\(I = 0\)) Short circuit (\(\Delta V_L = 0\))
Increasing \(R\)… Increases \(\tau\) (slower) Decreases \(\tau\) (faster)
\(R\) role Limits current flow Dissipates stored energy
Differential equation \(\mathcal{E} - q/C - IR = 0\) \(\mathcal{E} - IR - L\,dI/dt = 0\)

The physical reason for the inverted role of \(R\): In the RC circuit, the resistor is the bottleneck — it limits how fast charge can flow onto the capacitor. In the RL circuit, the inductor is the bottleneck — it limits how fast current can build. The resistor in the RL circuit is the “destination” that dissipates the stored magnetic energy during decay. Higher \(R\) means faster energy dissipation, hence shorter time constant.

Energy Stored in an Inductor

Work must be done against the back-EMF to establish current in an inductor. The instantaneous power delivered to the inductor is \(P = \mathcal{E}_L I = LI\,dI/dt\). Integrating from \(I = 0\) to \(I\):

\[\boxed{U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI^2}\]

This energy is stored in the magnetic field inside the inductor. For a solenoid with \(B = \mu_0 nI\) and volume \(V = \ell A\):

\[U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \frac{1}{2}(\mu_0 n^2 \ell A)I^2 = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\cdot(\ell A)\]

The magnetic energy density is:

\[\boxed{u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}}\]

Compare this to the electric energy density \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\) from Chapter 25. The structural parallel is exact:

Energy Density Electric (Ch 25) Magnetic (Ch 29)
Expression \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\) \(u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 H^2\)
Stored in Capacitor (parallel plates) Inductor (solenoid)
Field source Charge separation Current
Constant \(\varepsilon_0\) (permittivity) \(\mu_0\) (permeability)

In an electromagnetic wave (Chapter 31), the energy is shared equally between \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\): \(u_E = u_B\) at every point. This equipartition is not a coincidence — it is a consequence of Maxwell’s equations.

Example: Energy in an RL Circuit

\(\mathcal{E} = 24.0\ \text{V}\), \(R = 8.0\ \Omega\), \(L = 4.0\ \text{H}\).

(A) Time constant:

\[\tau = L/R = 4.0/8.0 = \boxed{0.50\ \text{s}}\]

(B) Steady-state current:

\[I_\text{max} = \mathcal{E}/R = 24.0/8.0 = \boxed{3.0\ \text{A}}\]

(C) Current at \(t = \tau\):

\[I(\tau) = 3.0(1 - e^{-1}) = 3.0(0.632) = \boxed{1.90\ \text{A}}\]

(D) Energy stored at steady state:

\[U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI_\text{max}^2 = \frac{1}{2}(4.0)(3.0)^2 = \boxed{18.0\ \text{J}}\]

(E) Power dissipated in \(R\) at \(t = \tau\):

\[P_R = I^2 R = (1.90)^2(8.0) = \boxed{28.8\ \text{W}}\]

Compare: at \(t = 0\), \(P_R = 0\) (no current yet). At \(t = \infty\), \(P_R = I_\text{max}^2 R = 72\ \text{W}\) (all battery power to resistor). The inductor stores no additional energy in steady state.

Example: Back-EMF in a Motor

A DC motor has inductance \(L = 50\ \text{mH}\) and winding resistance \(R = 2.0\ \Omega\). When running at full speed, it draws \(I = 3.0\ \text{A}\) from a \(12\ \text{V}\) supply. When the motor is suddenly switched off, the current must drop from 3.0 A to 0 A.

(A) Time constant for current decay:

\[\tau = L/R = 0.050/2.0 = \boxed{25\ \text{ms}}\]

(B) If an engineer tries to interrupt the current in \(\Delta t = 0.10\ \text{ms}\) (by opening a switch):

\[|\mathcal{E}_L| = L\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = (0.050)\frac{3.0}{1.0\times10^{-4}} = \boxed{1500\ \text{V}}\]

This is 125 times the supply voltage! The inductor generates whatever voltage is necessary to maintain current flow. In practice, this voltage arcs across the switch contacts, eroding them and creating electromagnetic interference. This is why inductive circuits always include a flyback diode or snubber circuit to provide a safe current path during switching. The inductor’s stored energy (\(U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = 0.225\ \text{J}\)) must go somewhere — the diode lets it dissipate gradually instead of catastrophically.

29.7 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Magnetic flux \(\Phi_B = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = BA\cos\theta\) measures how much magnetic field threads through a surface. SI unit: weber (Wb = T\(\cdot\)m\(^2\)).

  2. Faraday’s Law of Induction: A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an EMF: \(\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt\). The EMF is proportional to the rate of flux change, not to the flux itself.

  3. Lenz’s Law: The induced current opposes the change in flux that caused it. This is a consequence of energy conservation and is encoded in the negative sign of Faraday’s Law.

  4. Motional EMF: A conductor of length \(L\) moving at speed \(v\) through a field \(B\) develops \(\mathcal{E} = BLv\). This is Faraday’s Law applied to a changing-area circuit.

  5. Eddy currents are induced circulating currents in bulk conductors exposed to changing magnetic flux. They produce braking forces (magnetic braking) and resistive heating.

  6. Self-inductance \(L = N\Phi_B/I\) characterizes a coil’s ability to oppose changes in its own current. For a solenoid: \(L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A\). SI unit: henry (H).

  7. Mutual inductance \(M\) couples two coils: \(\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\,dI_1/dt\). It is the basis of the transformer.

  8. RL circuits have time constant \(\tau = L/R\). Current grows as \(I_\text{max}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})\) and decays as \(I_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\) — the exact mirror of RC circuits with the roles of voltage and current exchanged.

  9. Energy stored in an inductor: \(U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\). The magnetic energy density is \(u_B = B^2/(2\mu_0)\), the magnetic counterpart of \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\).

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Magnetic flux \(\Phi_B = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = BA\cos\theta\)
Faraday’s Law \(\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt\)

Self-inductance \(L = N\Phi_B/I\)
Solenoid inductance \(L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A = \mu_0 N^2 A/\ell\)

29.8 — Looking Back: Maxwell’s Equations Assembled

Faraday’s Law is the last new equation we need. For the first time, you can write all of classical electromagnetism on a single page. Here are Maxwell’s four equations in integral form, with the chapter where each piece entered our story:

\[\begin{array}{rl} \text{(1) Gauss's Law for } \vec{E}: & \displaystyle\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_\text{enc}}{\varepsilon_0} \\[0.6em] \text{(2) Gauss's Law for } \vec{B}: & \displaystyle\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0 \\[0.6em] \text{(3) Faraday's Law:} & \displaystyle\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} \\[0.6em] \text{(4) Amp\`ere-Maxwell Law:} & \displaystyle\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_\text{enc} + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \end{array}\]

Chapter Provenance

Equation What It Says First Encountered Completed In
(1) Gauss for \(\vec{E}\) Electric flux through a closed surface = \(Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0\) Ch 23 Ch 23
(2) Gauss for \(\vec{B}\) Net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero (no monopoles) Ch 28 §28.7 Ch 28 §28.7
(3) Faraday’s Law Changing magnetic flux drives a circulating electric field Ch 29 §29.2 Ch 29 §29.2 (this chapter)
(4) Ampère-Maxwell Law Currents and changing electric flux drive a circulating magnetic field Ch 28 §28.6 (static part) Ch 31 (displacement current)

The Unifying Grammar

Notice the shared vocabulary. Every one of the four equations is built from the same primitives:

  • Closed integrals — \(\oint\) over a surface (Eqs 1–2) or a loop (Eqs 3–4).
  • Flux — \(\Phi_E = \int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}\) or \(\Phi_B = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}\). Three of the four equations are statements about flux.
  • Rate of change — \(d\Phi/dt\) couples the two fields in Eqs 3 and 4. This coupling is what makes electromagnetic waves possible.

Eqs 1 and 2 are static statements: where the fields come from (charges) and where they don’t (no magnetic monopoles). Eqs 3 and 4 are dynamic statements: how the fields interconvert when things change. Every phenomenon in classical E&M — from a balloon sticking to a wall to the light from a distant star — is hidden inside these four lines.

What Each Chapter Bought You

Chapter Maxwell Contribution
Ch 22 Coulomb’s law → motivates \(\vec{E}\) as a field
Ch 23 Gauss’s Law for \(\vec{E}\) (Eq 1), electric flux \(\Phi_E\)
Ch 24–25 Potential, capacitance, energy density \(u_E\) (sidecar — not a Maxwell equation, but needed for EM-wave energy)
Ch 26–27 Current \(I\) and steady circuits (needed for Eq 4 RHS)
Ch 28 \(\vec{B}\) from currents; Gauss for \(\vec{B}\) (Eq 2); Ampère’s Law static form (Eq 4 partial)
Ch 29 Faraday’s Law (Eq 3); magnetic energy density \(u_B\); inductance as Faraday applied to self-flux
Ch 31 Displacement current completes Eq 4; EM waves follow directly

*Personal note: The four equations above are arguably the most beautiful result in classical physics. Feynman remarked that if all human knowledge were destroyed and only one sentence could be passed to the next generation, the sentence with the most information in the fewest words would be some form of “all things are made of atoms.” Maxwell’s equations come a close second — four lines that encode the behavior of light, the structure of atoms, every wire in every device you own, and the radiation crossing the universe. Now that you have all four, the rest of Chapter 31 will feel less like new material and more like consequences.

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 30, we turn from fields and circuits to light itself. Geometric optics — reflection, refraction, lenses, and mirrors — describes how light behaves when it encounters objects much larger than its wavelength. Wave optics — interference and diffraction — reveals what happens when light encounters structures comparable to its wavelength. Both regimes trace back to Maxwell’s equations, which unify the electric and magnetic phenomena we have been building across Chapters 22–29.

*Faraday’s Law is the third of Maxwell’s four equations. Together with Gauss’s Law, Gauss’s Law for magnetism, and Ampere’s Law (with Maxwell’s displacement current correction from Chapter 31), these four equations describe all of classical electromagnetism. Everything — from the static cling on a balloon to the light from a distant star — follows from them. What started with Coulomb’s single point charge in Chapter 22 has now grown into one of the most complete and beautiful theories in all of physics.
